claim: Intracranial EEG recordings were collected from sixteen patients presenting pharmaco-resistant focal epilepsy and undergoing presurgical evaluation (33.5±12.4 years old, 10 females).
source: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) recordings were collected from sixteen patients presenting pharmaco-resistant focal epilepsy and undergoing presurgical evaluation (33.5±12.4 years old, 10 females).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of patients, their condition, and demographic information.

claim: A total of 248 iEEG bipolar derivations located in the aINS, dlPFC, vmPFC, and lOFC regions were selected for analysis.
source: A total of 248 iEEG bipolar derivations located in the aINS, dlPFC, vmPFC, and lOFC regions (Figure 1A) and 1788 pairs of iEEG signals, both within and across brain regions (Figure 1B) were selected for further analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of bipolar derivations and their anatomical locations.

claim: 1788 pairs of iEEG signals, both within and across brain regions, were selected for analysis.
source: A total of 248 iEEG bipolar derivations located in the aINS, dlPFC, vmPFC, and lOFC regions (Figure 1A) and 1788 pairs of iEEG signals, both within and across brain regions (Figure 1B) were selected for further analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of signal pairs analyzed.

claim: Participants performed a probabilistic instrumental learning task to either maximize monetary gains or minimize monetary losses.
source: Participants performed a probabilistic instrumental learning task and had to choose between two cues to either maximize monetary gains (for reward cues) or minimize monetary losses (for punishment cues) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral task performed by participants.

claim: The task structure was designed so that the number of trials was balanced between reward and punishment conditions.
source: Overall, they selected more monetary gains and avoided monetary losses but the task structure was designed so that the number of trials was balanced between reward and punishment conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the task design feature regarding trial balance.

claim: Trial-wise prediction errors were estimated by fitting a Q-learning model to behavioral data.
source: We estimated trial-wise prediction errors by fitting a Q-learning model to behavioral data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational method used to estimate prediction errors.

claim: The Q-learning model used three constant parameters: learning rate α, choice temperature β, and Ө parameter.
source: We used three constant parameters: (i) the learning rate α accounting for how fast participants learned new pairs of cues; (ii) the choice temperature β to model different levels of exploration and exploitation; (iii) Ө parameter to account for the tendency to repeat the choice made in the previous trial.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists the three parameters used in the Q-learning model.

claim: RPE and PPE showed high absolute values early during learning and tended toward zero as participants learned to predict the outcome.
source: RPE and PPE showed high absolute values early during learning and tended toward zero as participants learned to predict the outcome (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics of prediction errors, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: The frequency range significantly encoding prediction errors was between 50 and 100 Hz.
source: Preliminary spectrally-resolved analyses showed that the frequency range significantly encoding prediction errors was between 50 and 100 Hz (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the frequency range based on spectral analysis, supported by a supplementary figure.

claim: All four cortical regions (aINS, dlPFC, lOFC, vmPFC) displayed significant group-level effects in mutual information between gamma power and prediction error signals.
source: MI analysis between gamma power and prediction error signals displayed significant group-level effects in all four cortical regions (Figure 2A) and globally reproduced previous findings based on general linear model analyses (Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript reports significant effects across all regions, referencing both current data and prior work.

claim: The vmPFC and dlPFC displayed complementary functional preferences for RPE and PPE, respectively.
source: Whereas the vmPFC and dlPFC displayed complementary functional preferences for RPE and PPE, respectively, the aINS and the lOFC carried similar amounts of information about both R/PPE (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional preferences of different brain regions based on MI analysis.

claim: The aINS and lOFC carried similar amounts of information about both RPE and PPE.
source: Whereas the vmPFC and dlPFC displayed complementary functional preferences for RPE and PPE, respectively, the aINS and the lOFC carried similar amounts of information about both R/PPE (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional properties of aINS and lOFC based on MI analysis.

claim: All regions displayed a local mixed encoding of prediction errors with temporal dynamics peaking around 500 ms after outcome presentation.
source: All regions displayed a local mixed encoding of prediction errors with temporal dynamics peaking around 500 ms after outcome presentation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal characteristics of PE encoding across regions.

claim: The vmPFC and dlPFC contained approximately 30% of RPE- and PPE-specific contacts, respectively.
source: The vmPFC and dlPFC differentially responded to reward and punishment PEs, and contained approximately 30% of RPE- and PPE-specific contacts, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript quantifies the proportion of specific contacts in these regions.

claim: All regions contained approximately 10% of PE-unspecific bipolar derivations that responded to both RPE and PPE.
source: Importantly, all regions contained approximately 10% of PE-unspecific bipolar derivations that responded to both RPE and PPE, especially in the aINS and dlPFC.
evidence: The manuscript quantifies the proportion of non-specific contacts across regions.

claim: RPE- and PPE-specific analyses exclusively showed negative modulations of interaction information, indicating the presence of redundancy-dominated local and long-range interactions.
source: RPE- and PPE-specific analyses exclusively showed negative modulations of II, therefore, indicating the presence of redundancy-dominated local and long-range interactions (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the sign of II modulations and interprets them as redundancy-dominated interactions.

claim: Significant RPE-specific interactions were exclusively observed in the vmPFC and lOFC within-region analyses.
source: Within-region II analyses showed that significant RPE-specific interactions were exclusively observed in the vmPFC and lOFC, whereas PPE-specific interactions were present only in the dlPFC.
evidence: The manuscript describes the regional specificity of RPE interactions in within-region analysis.

claim: PPE-specific interactions were present only in the dlPFC in within-region analyses.
source: Within-region II analyses showed that significant RPE-specific interactions were exclusively observed in the vmPFC and lOFC, whereas PPE-specific interactions were present only in the dlPFC.
evidence: The manuscript describes the regional specificity of PPE interactions in within-region analysis.

claim: The aINS displayed both RPE- and PPE-specific interactions in within-region analyses.
source: In addition, the aINS was found to display both RPE- and PPE-specific interactions (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the mixed interaction profile of the aINS.

claim: RPE-specific interactions were observed between the lOFC and vmPFC in between-region analyses.
source: RPE-specific interactions were observed between the lOFC and vmPFC, whereas PPE-specific interactions were observed between the aINS and dlPFC and to a smaller extent between the dlPFC and lOFC, peaking at 500 ms after outcome presentation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the between-region RPE-specific interactions.

claim: PPE-specific interactions were observed between the aINS and dlPFC, peaking at 500 ms after outcome presentation.
source: RPE-specific interactions were observed between the lOFC and vmPFC, whereas PPE-specific interactions were observed between the aINS and dlPFC and to a smaller extent between the dlPFC and lOFC, peaking at 500 ms after outcome presentation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the between-region PPE-specific interactions and their timing.

claim: A significant difference between RPE and PPE was exclusively observed in the lOFC-vmPFC and aINS-dlPFC interactions.
source: A significant difference between RPE and PPE was exclusively observed in the lOFC-vmPFC and aINS-dlPFC interactions, but not between dlPFC and lOFC (green clusters in Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical differences between RPE and PPE in specific region pairs.

claim: A maximum delay of information transfer between pairs of signals comprised an interval between 116 and 236 ms.
source: Delay-specific analyses of TE showed that a maximum delay of information transfer between pairs of signals comprised an interval between 116 and 236 ms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the delay range for information transfer based on TE analysis.

claim: The TE from the aINS to the dlPFC peaked at approximately 400 ms after outcome onset and was significantly stronger during the punishment condition compared to the rewarding condition.
source: We observed that the TE from the aINS to the dlPFC (TEaINS→dlPFC) peaked at approximately 400 ms after outcome onset and was significantly stronger during the punishment condition compared to the rewarding condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the timing and condition-specific modulation of TE from aINS to dlPFC.

claim: The information flow around ~800 ms from the vmPFC to the lOFC was significantly stronger during the rewarding condition.
source: By contrast, the information flow around ~800 ms from the vmPFC to the lOFC (TEvmPFC→lOFC) was significantly stronger during the rewarding condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the timing and condition-specific modulation of TE from vmPFC to lOFC.

claim: No other brain interactions besides aINS→dlPFC and vmPFC→lOFC were found significant in transfer entropy analysis.
source: No other brain interactions were found significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no other interactions showed significant TE modulations.

claim: Encoding of PEs was specifically associated with significantly positive interaction information between the dlPFC and vmPFC.
source: Encoding of PEs was specifically associated with significantly positive II between the dlPFC and vmPFC (IIdlPFC-vmPFC Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports positive II between dlPFC and vmPFC for full PE encoding.

claim: The synergistic interaction between dlPFC and vmPFC occurred approximately between 250 and 600 ms after outcome onset.
source: Such between-regions synergy-dominated interaction occurred approximately between 250 and 600 ms after outcome onset.
evidence: The manuscript reports the timing of the synergistic interaction.

claim: Significant synergistic interactions were found between recordings with mixed specificity (IIPPE-RPE and IIMixed) between 250 and 600ms after outcome onset.
source: Interestingly, we found significant synergistic interactions between recordings with mixed specificity i.e., IIPPE-RPE and IIMixed between 250 and 600ms after outcome onset (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports synergistic interactions for specific categories of local specificity.

claim: Reward and punishment learning are two key facets of human and animal behavior that grant successful adaptation to changes in the environment and avoidance of potential harm.
source: Reward and punishment learning are two key facets of human and animal behavior, because they grant successful adaptation to changes in the environment and avoidance of potential harm.
evidence: The manuscript states the functional importance of reward and punishment learning.

claim: Reward and punishment learning abilities are formalized by the law of effect.
source: These learning abilities are formalized by the law of effect (Thorndike, 1898; Bouton, 2007) and they pertain the goal-directed system, which supports the acquisition of action-outcome contingencies and the selection of actions according to expected outcomes, as well as current goal and motivational state (Dickinson and Balleine, 1994; Balleine and Dickinson, 1998; Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Balleine, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites the law of effect and related literature on goal-directed learning.

claim: Reward prediction error signals have been observed in the midbrain, ventral striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
source: Reward prediction error (RPE) signals have been observed in the midbrain, ventral striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) (Schultz et al., 1997; O'Doherty et al., 2004; O'Doherty et al., 2001; Pessiglione et al., 2006; D'Ardenne et al., 2008; Steinberg et al., 2013; Palminteri et al., 2015; Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies reporting RPE signals in specific brain regions.

claim: Punishment prediction error signals have been found in the anterior insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and amygdala.
source: Punishment prediction error (PPE) signals have been found in the anterior insula (aINS), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC), and amygdala (O'Doherty et al., 2001; Seymour et al., 2005; Pessiglione et al., 2006; Yacubian et al., 2006; Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies reporting PPE signals in specific brain regions.

claim: Evidence from pharmacological manipulations and lesion studies indicates that reward and punishment learning can be selectively affected.
source: Evidence from pharmacological manipulations and lesion studies also indicates that reward and punishment learning can be selectively affected (Frank et al., 2004; Bódi et al., 2009; Palminteri et al., 2009; Palminteri et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing selective effects on reward and punishment learning.

claim: Hubs of the reward circuit, such as the midbrain dopamine systems and vmPFC, contain neural populations encoding also punishments.
source: Indeed, hubs of the reward circuit, such as the midbrain dopamine systems and vmPFC, contain neural populations encoding also punishments (Tom et al., 2007; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Plassmann et al., 2010; Monosov and Hikosaka, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing mixed encoding in reward-related regions.

claim: Learning reflects a network phenomenon emerging from neural interactions distributed over cortical-subcortical circuits.
source: To address this issue, we repose on recent literature proposing that learning reflects a network phenomenon emerging from neural interactions distributed over cortical-subcortical circuits (Bassett and Mattar, 2017; Hunt and Hayden, 2017; Averbeck and Murray, 2020; Averbeck and O'Doherty, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent literature proposing a network-based view of learning.

claim: Cognitive functions emerge from the dynamic coordination over large-scale and hierarchically organized networks.
source: Indeed, cognitive functions emerge from the dynamic coordination over large-scale and hierarchically organized networks (Varela et al., 2001; Bressler and Menon, 2010; Reid et al., 2019; Panzeri et al., 2022; Thiebaut de Schotten and Forkel, 2022; Miller et al., 2024; Noble et al., 2024) and accumulating evidence supports that information about task variables is widely distributed across brain circuits, rather than anatomically localized (Parras et al., 2017; Saleem et al., 2018; Steinmetz et al., 2019; Urai et al., 2022; Voitov and Mrsic-Flogel, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting the network-based view of cognitive functions.

claim: A trade-off between redundancy for robust sensory and motor functions and synergistic interaction may be important for flexible higher cognition.
source: The search for synergy- and redundancy-dominated interactions is motivated by recent hypotheses suggesting that a trade-off between redundancy for robust sensory and motor functions and synergistic interaction may be important for flexible higher cognition (Luppi et al., 2024).
evidence: The manuscript cites a hypothesis about the functional role of redundancy and synergy.

claim: Synergistic interactions have been reported between distant transmodal regions during high-level cognition.
source: Indeed, synergistic interactions have been reported between distant transmodal regions during high-level cognition (Luppi et al., 2022) and, at the microscale, in populations of neurons within a cortical column of the visual cortex and across areas of the visuomotor network (Nigam et al., 2019; Varley et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies reporting synergistic interactions in different contexts.

claim: The vmPFC was the only region to show a higher group-level preference for RPEs.
source: Amongst the four investigated core-learning regions, the vmPFC was the only region to show a higher group-level preference for RPEs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional preference of vmPFC based on the analysis results.

claim: The vmPFC is functionally more specialized for the processing outcomes in reward learning, as previously put forward by human fMRI meta-analyses.
source: This supports the notion that the vmPFC is functionally more specialized for the processing outcomes in reward learning, as previously put forward by human fMRI meta-analyses (Yacubian et al., 2006; Diekhof et al., 2012; Bartra et al., 2013; Garrison et al., 2013; Fouragnan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the vmPFC results in the context of prior fMRI literature.

claim: The dlPFC showed a stronger selectivity for punishment PE, supporting results from fMRI studies showing selective activations for aversive outcomes.
source: The dlPFC, instead, showed a stronger selectivity for punishment PE, thus supporting results from fMRI studies showing selective activations for aversive outcomes (Liu et al., 2011; Garrison et al., 2013; Fouragnan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the dlPFC results in the context of prior fMRI literature.

claim: The aINS carried a comparable amount of information about the RPE and PPE, suggesting that the insula is part of the surprise-encoding network.
source: The aINS carried a comparable amount of information about the RPE and PPE, thus suggesting that the insula is part of the surprise-encoding network (Fouragnan et al., 2018; Loued-Khenissi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the aINS results and cites supporting literature.

claim: The lOFC showed an initial temporal selectivity for PPE followed by a delayed one about the RPE.
source: The lOFC showed an initial temporal selectivity for PPE followed by a delayed one about the RPE.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics of lOFC encoding.

claim: The lOFC was activated when receiving punishing outcomes, but also contains reward-related information.
source: This is in accordance with fMRI and human intracranial studies which revealed that the lOFC was activated when receiving punishing outcomes, but also contains reward-related information (O'Doherty et al., 2001; Saez et al., 2018; Gueguen et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies supporting the mixed encoding in lOFC.

claim: 5 to 20% of contacts within a given region encoded both the RPE and PPE, revealing local mixed representations.
source: Interestingly, we observed that 5 to 20% of contacts within a given region encoded both the RPE and PPE, thus revealing local mixed representations.
evidence: The manuscript quantifies the proportion of mixed-encoding contacts.

claim: The human prefrontal cortex exhibits a mixed local selectivity for prediction error signals at the mesoscopic scale.
source: These results suggest that the human prefrontal cortex exhibits a mixed local selectivity for prediction error signals at the mesoscopic scale.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the mixed encoding results as evidence for mixed selectivity.

claim: The prefrontal cortex contains single neurons exhibiting mixed selectivity for multiple task variables.
source: This view is in line with recent literature showing that the prefrontal cortex contains single neurons exhibiting mixed selectivity for multiple task variables (Meyers et al., 2008; Rigotti et al., 2013; Stokes et al., 2013; Panzeri et al., 2015; Parthasarathy et al., 2017; Bernardi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on mixed selectivity at the single-neuron level.

claim: Single-unit studies have reported neurons encoding both rewarding and aversive outcomes in the OFC of the primate.
source: In the learning domain, single-unit studies have reported neurons encoding both rewarding and aversive outcomes in the OFC of the primate (Morrison and Salzman, 2009; Monosov and Hikosaka, 2012; Hirokawa et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites single-unit studies showing mixed encoding in OFC.

claim: Mixed selectivity provides computational benefits, such as increasing the number of binary classifications, improving cognitive flexibility, and simplifying readout by downstream neurons.
source: Mixed selectivity provides computational benefits, such as increasing the number of binary classifications, improving cognitive flexibility, and simplifying readout by downstream neurons (Fusi et al., 2016; Helfrich and Knight, 2019; Ohnuki et al., 2021; Panzeri et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the computational benefits of mixed selectivity.

claim: The interaction information revealed redundancy-dominated interactions specific for RPE and PPE in the vmPFC and the dlPFC, respectively.
source: The II revealed redundancy-dominated interactions specific for RPE and PPE in the vmPFC and the dlPFC, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of II analysis for within-region interactions.

claim: The aINS was the only region for which the between-contacts II did not increase the functional selectivity, with large redundant interactions for both RPE and PPE signals.
source: The aINS was the only region for which the between-contacts II did not increase the functional selectivity, with large redundant interactions for both RPE and PPE signals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the unique interaction profile of the aINS.

claim: Within-area redundant interactions can potentially amplify the functional specificity, despite the presence of local mixed selectivity.
source: This suggests that within-area redundant interactions can potentially amplify the functional specificity, despite the presence of local mixed selectivity (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript infers a functional role for within-area redundant interactions.

claim: Across-areas interaction information revealed two subsystems with redundancy-dominated interactions: a reward subsystem with RPE-specific interactions between the lOFC and vmPFC, and a punishment subsystem with PPE-specific interactions between the aINS and dlPFC.
source: Across-areas interaction information revealed two subsystems with redundancy-dominated interactions. A reward subsystem with RPE-specific interactions between the lOFC and vmPFC, and a punishment subsystem with PPE-specific interactions between the aINS and dlPFC (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of two distinct subsystems based on II analysis.

claim: The observed functionally-distinct learning circuits for RPE and PPEs are associated with differential cortico-cortical interactions, rather than distinct local properties.
source: This result suggests that the observed functionally-distinct learning circuits for RPE and PPEs are associated with differential cortico-cortical interactions, rather than distinct local properties.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the interaction results as evidence for network-level functional specificity.

claim: Redundancy-based network-level interactions are related to the functional specificity observed in neuroimaging and lesion studies.
source: More generally, our results suggest that redundancy-based network-level interactions are related to the functional specificity observed in neuroimaging and lesion studies (Pessiglione and Delgado, 2015; Palminteri and Pessiglione, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the results in the context of prior neuroimaging and lesion literature.

claim: Within the reward subsystem, the vmPFC played a driving role toward the lOFC only during the rewarding condition.
source: Within the reward subsystem, the vmPFC played a driving role toward the lOFC only during the rewarding condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the directional relationship within the reward subsystem based on TE analysis.

claim: Within the punishment subsystem, the aINS played a driving role toward the dlPFC only during the punishment condition.
source: Conversely, within the punishment subsystem, the aINS played a driving role toward the dlPFC only during the punishment condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the directional relationship within the punishment subsystem based on TE analysis.

claim: Redundancy-dominated cognitive networks are associated with the occurrence of information-routing capabilities, where signals are communicated on top of collective reference states.
source: These results support the notion that redundancy-dominated cognitive networks are associated with the occurrence of information-routing capabilities, where signals are communicated on top of collective reference states (Battaglia and Brovelli, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the TE results in the context of a theoretical framework.

claim: Tract tracing studies in the macaque have revealed strong interconnections between the lOFC and vmPFC.
source: Tract tracing studies in the macaque have revealed strong interconnections between the lOFC and vmPFC in the macaque (Carmichael and Price, 1996; Ongür and Price, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites anatomical studies in non-human primates.

claim: Several studies found strong probabilities of structural connectivity between the anterior insula with the orbitofrontal cortex and the dorsolateral part of the prefrontal cortex in humans.
source: Several studies found strong probabilities of structural connectivity between the anterior insula with the orbitofrontal cortex and the dorsolateral part of the prefrontal cortex (Cloutman et al., 2012; Ghaziri et al., 2017), and between the lOFC and vmPFC (Heather Hsu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites human dMRI studies showing structural connectivity.

claim: The statistical dependency between the LFP of distant areas could be potentially explained by direct anatomical connections.
source: In addition, the statistical dependency (e.g. coherence) between the LFP of distant areas could be potentially explained by direct anatomical connections (Schneider et al., 2021; Vinck et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies linking functional and structural connectivity.

claim: Drug-resistant epileptic patients with resected insula showed poorer performance than healthy controls in case of risky loss compared to risky gains.
source: Our results are further supported by a recent study involving drug-resistant epileptic patients with resected insula who showed poorer performance than healthy controls in case of risky loss compared to risky gains (Von Siebenthal et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a lesion study supporting the role of the insula in punishment processing.

claim: The encoding of global PE signals was associated with synergy-dominated interactions between the two subsystems, mediated by the interactions between the dlPFC and the vmPFC.
source: We found that the encoding of global PE signals was associated with synergy-dominated interactions between the two subsystems, mediated by the interactions between the dlPFC and the vmPFC (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports synergistic interactions for global PE encoding.

claim: Synergy-dominated interaction reveals that the joint representation of the dlPFC and vmPFC is greater than the sum of their individual contributions to the encoding of global PE signals.
source: Importantly, such synergy-dominated interaction reveals that the joint representation of the dlPFC and vmPFC is greater than the sum of their individual contributions to the encoding of global PE signals.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the meaning of synergistic interactions.

claim: Successful adaptation in varying contexts requires both the vmPFC and dlPFC for the encoding of global PE signals.
source: Thus, it suggests that successful adaptation in varying contexts requires both the vmPFC and dlPFC for the encoding of global PE signals.
evidence: The manuscript infers a functional role for the synergistic interaction.

claim: Redundant interactions are predominantly associated with structurally coupled and functionally segregated processing.
source: By combining functional and diffusion MRI, recent work suggested that redundant interactions are predominantly associated with structurally coupled and functionally segregated processing.
evidence: The manuscript cites recent work on the relationship between redundancy and brain organization.

claim: Synergistic interactions preferentially support functional integrative processes and complex cognition across higher-order brain networks.
source: In contrast, synergistic interactions preferentially support functional integrative processes and complex cognition across higher-order brain networks (Luppi et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites work on the role of synergistic interactions in cognition.

claim: Triadic synergistic interactions between the continuous spike counts recorded within and across areas of the visuomotor network carry behaviorally-relevant information and display the strongest modulations during the processing of visual information and movement execution.
source: Triadic synergistic interactions between the continuous spike counts recorded within and across areas of the visuomotor network have been shown to carry behaviorally-relevant information and to display the strongest modulations during the processing of visual information and movement execution (Varley et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on synergistic interactions in the visuomotor system.

claim: Cortical representations of prediction error signals in the acoustic domain observed tone-related and instantaneous redundant interactions, such as time-lagged synergistic interactions within and across temporal and frontal regions of the auditory system.
source: Finally, cortical representations of prediction error signals in the acoustic domain observed tone-related and instantaneous redundant interactions, such as time-lagged synergistic interactions within and across temporal and frontal regions of the auditory system (Gelens et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on redundant and synergistic interactions in the auditory system.

claim: The amount of information encoded by a population of neurons can be modulated by pairwise and higher-order interactions, producing varying fractions of redundancy and synergy.
source: At the microscopic level, the amount of information encoded by a population of neurons can be modulated by pairwise and higher-order interactions, producing varying fractions of redundancy and synergy (Averbeck et al., 2006; Panzeri et al., 2015; Panzeri et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on redundancy and synergy at the neuronal population level.

claim: Redundant coding is intricately linked to correlated activity and can spontaneously emerge due to the spatial correlations present in natural scenes by triggering neurons with overlapping receptive fields.
source: Redundant coding is intricately linked to correlated activity (Gutnisky and Dragoi, 2008) and can spontaneously emerge due to the spatial correlations present in natural scenes by triggering neurons with overlapping receptive fields.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and describes mechanisms of redundant coding.

claim: Correlations between the trial-by-trial variations of neuronal responses could limit the amount of information encoded by a population and facilitate readout by downstream neurons.
source: Correlations between the trial-by-trial variations of neuronal responses could limit the amount of information encoded by a population (Bartolo et al., 2020; Kafashan et al., 2021) and facilitate readout by downstream neurons (Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the effects of neuronal correlations.

claim: A study reported synergistic coding in a V1 cortical column together with structured correlations between synergistic and redundant hubs.
source: Recently, a study reported synergistic coding in a V1 cortical column together with structured correlations between synergistic and redundant hubs (Nigam et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on synergistic coding in V1.

claim: Population codes with balancing proportions of redundancy and synergy offer a good compromise between system robustness and resilience to cell loss and the creation of new information.
source: Taken together, we suggest that population codes with balancing proportions of redundancy and synergy offer a good compromise between system robustness and resilience to cell loss and the creation of new information (Panzeri et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a functional interpretation of redundancy-synergy balance, citing supporting literature.

claim: Redundancy-dominated interactions confer robustness and network-level selectivity for complementary learning processes, which may lead to functional integration processes.
source: We suggest that redundancy-dominated interactions confer robustness and network-level selectivity for complementary learning processes, which may lead to functional integration processes.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a functional role for redundancy-dominated interactions based on the results.

claim: Synergy-dominated interactions seem to support neural interactions between redundancy-dominated networks, thus supporting functional integrative processes in the brain.
source: On the other hand, synergy-dominated interactions seem to support neural interactions between redundancy-dominated networks, thus supporting functional integrative processes in the brain.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a functional role for synergy-dominated interactions based on the results.

claim: Redundant and synergistic interactions occur across multiple spatial scales from local to large-scale.
source: In addition, our study suggests that redundant and synergistic interactions occur across multiple spatial scales from local to large-scale.
evidence: The manuscript infers a general principle about the spatial organization of interactions.

claim: Functional specialization for reward and punishment PE signals occurs with redundancy-dominated interactions within the two subsystems formed by the vmPFC-lOFC and aINS-dlPFC, respectively.
source: Instead, we propose that functional specialization for reward and punishment PE signals occurs with redundancy-dominated interactions within the two subsystems formed by the vmPFC-lOFC and aINS-dlPFC, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a model of functional specialization based on the results.

claim: Within each subsystem, asymmetric and directional interactions were observed with the vmPFC and aINS playing a driving role in the reward and punishment learning circuits.
source: Within each subsystem, we observed asymmetric and directional interactions with the vmPFC and aINS playing a driving role in the reward and punishment learning circuits.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the directional interaction findings.

claim: Switching between reward and punishment learning was supported by synergistic collaboration between subsystems.
source: Finally, switching between reward and punishment learning was supported by synergistic collaboration between subsystems.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the synergistic interaction findings.

claim: Higher-order integration between functionally-distinct subsystems are mediated by synergistic interactions.
source: This supports the idea that higher-order integration between functionally-distinct subsystems are mediated by synergistic interactions.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a general principle about integration based on the results.

claim: The results provide a unifying view reconciling distributed cortical representations with interactions supporting reward and punishment learning.
source: Taken together, our results provide a unifying view reconciling distributed cortical representations with interactions supporting reward and punishment learning.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the overall contribution of the study.

claim: The results highlight the relevance of considering learning as a network-level phenomenon by linking distributed and functionally redundant subnetworks through synergistic interactions hence supporting flexible cognition.
source: They highlight the relevance of considering learning as a network-level phenomenon by linking distributed and functionally redundant subnetworks through synergistic interactions hence supporting flexible cognition (Fedorenko and Thompson-Schill, 2014; Petersen and Sporns, 2015; Bassett and Mattar, 2017; Hunt and Hayden, 2017; Averbeck and Murray, 2020; Averbeck and O'Doherty, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the theoretical implications of the study, citing supporting literature.

claim: Multi-lead and semi-rigid depth electrodes were stereotactically implanted according to the suspected origin of seizures.
source: Multi-lead and semi-rigid depth electrodes were stereotactically implanted according to the suspected origin of seizures.
